title: React Event Handling
intro: From a student’s click to an application’s response.

blocks.title: Our classroom example
blocks.text: A student portal: register for classes, search for classmates and scroll through student lists.

blocks.title: What we will learn
blocks.text: Events and handlers; mouse, keyboard and forms; controlled inputs; event objects; bubbling; debounce and throttle.

key: Small user actions make a website interactive.
notes: Introduce yourself and GROUP 8. Ask classmates what happens when they click Register on a student website. A page is not interactive just because it has a button: code needs to respond to the click. Explain that we will follow familiar student activities rather than memorise definitions. By the end, we should be able to describe how input reaches a handler and how React updates the screen. Transition: first, name the parts involved in a click.

title: Events, handlers and responses
intro: An event is something that happens on a page, such as a click, a key press or a change in an input. Event handling means running code in response to that action.

blocks.title: Event
blocks.text: The student clicks Register. The click is the event; it tells the application that something happened.

blocks.title: Event handler
blocks.text: A function that React runs for an event. It can check information, update state or show a message.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.text: Handlers connect the student’s actions to useful responses. Without them, a page cannot respond to many user actions.

key: Event = what happened. Handler = the function that responds.
notes: Begin with a doorbell: pressing it is an event, and someone answering is the response. On a website, a click is an event and a JavaScript function is the handler. React connects the action to that function using a JSX event prop. A handler might display a registration message or start a request; the click itself does not automatically register anyone. In our next example, the response is only a local message, not a real registration service. Transition to connecting a handler in JSX.

title: Connect a Register button
intro: JSX is the HTML-like markup we write inside a React component. Use onClick to give React the function it should run when the button is clicked.

blocks.title: 1 · Remember the message
blocks.text: useState stores a message. The setter changes it and asks React to update the screen.

blocks.title: 2 · Pass the function
blocks.text: onClick={handleRegister} passes the function. Writing handleRegister() would call it while rendering instead.

blocks.title: 3 · Display the response
blocks.text: After the click, the paragraph shows “Registration received!” from the updated state.

key: Pass a handler function; let React call it when the event happens.
notes: Introduce the component as a reusable piece of the screen. Walk through the import, then the empty message stored by useState. Defining handleRegister does not run it yet. The button’s onClick gives React a reference to the function. When clicked, React calls the function, the setter changes the message, and React renders the new paragraph. Explain that braces insert JavaScript into JSX. This demonstrates the response, not saving a student record. Ask: why is there no pair of parentheses after handleRegister in onClick? Transition to the whole sequence.

title: Follow the click
intro: A click does not change the screen by itself. The handler decides the response, and a state update gives React new information to display.

blocks.title: React receives the event
blocks.text: React gives the handler an event object if the handler needs information about the action.

blocks.title: The screen updates
blocks.text: The setter requests another render. React uses the new state to update the message on screen.

key: User action → handler → state update → updated screen.
notes: Point to the steps from left to right. The student presses Register. React sees the click and calls the connected function. That function changes the message using the setter. React then renders the component with the new message. State is not changed by directly editing the paragraph. Also explain that not every handler updates state: some may navigate, prevent a browser action or log information. Transition: there are several kinds of mouse actions, not only clicks.

title: Mouse events: click and hover
intro: Mouse events let a page respond to actions made with a pointer. In a student portal, different mouse actions can have different meanings.

blocks.title: onClick
blocks.text: Runs after a click. Example: click Register to send the form or click a course to select it.

blocks.title: onDoubleClick
blocks.text: Runs for a double-click. Example: open a student card in an editing view. A double-click also produces click events.

blocks.title: onMouseEnter / onMouseLeave
blocks.text: Enter runs when the pointer enters an item; leave runs when it exits. Example: show extra course information, then hide it.

key: Choose an event that matches the action the student is making.
notes: Introduce a student course card. One click can select the card; a double-click can open editing. Explain the difference between hovering and clicking: onMouseEnter responds without a button press, and onMouseLeave responds when the pointer exits. A double-click can also trigger onClick, so do not attach conflicting actions without thinking about their relationship. Important information should not be available only through hover, since touch and keyboard users need access too. Transition to the press and release parts of a click.

title: Mouse events: press and release
intro: A mouse click includes pressing a button down and releasing it. React can respond to each part separately when the interface needs that detail.

blocks.title: onMouseDown
blocks.text: Runs when a mouse button is pressed. Example: start showing a pressed state on a course card.

blocks.title: onMouseUp
blocks.text: Runs when the mouse button is released over the element. Example: remove the pressed state.

blocks.title: onClick
blocks.text: Usually follows a press and release that completes a click. Example: select the course once the click is complete.

key: Down = press. Up = release. Click = completed click.
notes: Demonstrate with your hand pressing and releasing a mouse button. Down is the start; up is the release; click is the completed activation. This order describes a common click, not a guarantee for every interaction. If the pointer is released outside the element, its onMouseUp may not run. Robust drag interactions often use pointer events and pointer capture, but we are keeping this lesson focused on mouse event meanings. These examples describe visible feedback, not a complete drag system. Transition to a small hover code example.

title: Show course details on hover
intro: The handlers change state, and the component uses that state to decide whether to show the extra information.

blocks.title: State
blocks.text: showInfo starts as false, so only the course title is visible.

blocks.title: Enter and leave
blocks.text: Entering sets true. Leaving sets false. Each setter asks React to update the screen.

blocks.title: Visible result
blocks.text: The && expression shows the paragraph only when showInfo is true.

key: A handler changes data; React uses that data to display the result.
notes: Explain the small code line by line. The state is a yes-or-no value. The two arrow functions are handlers passed to React; they run later when the corresponding event occurs. The conditional expression displays the extra paragraph when the condition is true. The section is an HTML element grouping course information. For a real portal, also make the information available through focus or a click for users without a mouse. Transition: students can interact with a keyboard as well.

title: Keyboard events
intro: Keyboard events report key actions on the focused element. Focus means that the element is currently ready to receive keyboard input.

blocks.title: onKeyDown
blocks.text: Runs when a key is pressed down. Holding a key can produce repeated keydown events.

blocks.title: onKeyUp
blocks.text: Runs when the key is released. It is different from the initial press.

blocks.title: event.key
blocks.text: Tells us which key was involved, such as "Enter", "Escape" or "a". Use it to choose a response.

key: KeyDown detects a press; KeyUp detects a release.
notes: Ask students to click a search field so it has focus, then press and release Enter. Keydown happens at the press; keyup at release. The handler receives an event object whose key property names the key. Holding a letter may produce repeated keydown events, so it is not always one event per physical press. These events are useful for keyboard commands; onChange is usually the right way to track text, including paste and other input methods. Transition to searching with Enter.

title: Press Enter to search
intro: A student types a name, then presses Enter. The handler checks event.key before responding, so other keys do not start the search.

blocks.title: Identify the key
blocks.text: The if condition matches "Enter". Other keys do not run the search response.

blocks.title: Read the text
blocks.text: event.currentTarget is the input whose handler is running. Its value is the current search text.

blocks.title: Show the example response
blocks.text: This example displays the query in an alert. A real portal would pass it to a search function.

key: Use event.key to respond to a specific key.
notes: Start with a student typing Sara. Each letter can cause keyboard events, but the condition ignores them. When Enter is pressed, the condition is true and the alert displays the field’s text. currentTarget points to the element with this handler; here it is the input. This is an uncontrolled field used for a simple keyboard example; we will soon learn controlled fields. A real search service would replace the alert. If the field belongs to a form, form submission is usually the best way to support Enter and the submit button together. Transition to form events.

title: Form events: type and submit
intro: A registration form collects a student’s name, email and registration number. React handlers can respond while the student edits the fields and when the form is submitted.

blocks.title: onChange
blocks.text: For a text input, React runs it as the value changes. Example: keep the student’s name in state as they type.

blocks.title: onSubmit
blocks.text: Runs on the form when it is submitted, such as by a submit button or Enter. Use it to check the data and respond.

blocks.title: Why use both?
blocks.text: onChange tracks the information; onSubmit decides what to do with the completed form.

key: Track editing with onChange; handle the complete form with onSubmit.
notes: Introduce the registration form as a container for several fields. onChange is not only about pressing keys: pasted text can change the input too. onSubmit belongs on the form rather than only on the button, so keyboard submission follows the same logic. Developers may validate required fields and then send data to a service. A state update alone does not save information permanently. Transition to moving between fields.

title: Form events: focus and blur
intro: Focus tells us which field the student is using. Blur tells us that the field has lost focus, often because the student moved to another field.

blocks.title: onFocus
blocks.text: Runs when a field receives focus. Example: show a hint about the required registration-number format.

blocks.title: onBlur
blocks.text: Runs when a field loses focus. Example: check whether an email is missing or has an invalid format.

blocks.title: Student’s journey
blocks.text: Focus the name field, type a name, move to email, then submit. Several different events happen during this journey.

key: Focus = entering a field. Blur = leaving a field.
notes: Explain focus using the blinking text cursor. Clicking a field or using Tab can focus it. When the student moves to email, the name field blurs and email receives focus. A hint on focus helps before a mistake; a validation message on blur can avoid interrupting every keystroke. Validation is a developer’s choice: blur does not validate automatically. Transition to a complete short form example.

title: A student registration form
intro: The form collects three values and handles submission in one place. Browser checks run for required fields and the email input before a normal submit event.

blocks.title: Fields
blocks.text: name attributes identify the values. required asks the browser to reject empty fields.

blocks.title: Submit handler
blocks.text: preventDefault stops normal form navigation. FormData reads the submitted values from this form.

blocks.title: Practice response
blocks.text: The alert confirms the student’s name. Saving to a real portal needs a separate service.

key: Handle submission on the form, not just the button.
notes: Introduce this as a short form using browser-held input values so we can focus on submission. The event’s currentTarget is the form. preventDefault stops its usual navigation. FormData collects the named fields; get returns the name value. Name, email and registration number are required, and type=email gives a basic browser email check. Explain that required does not guarantee a valid registration number and a real application needs further validation. The alert is a demonstration, not persistent registration. Transition: now let React keep each field’s value in state.

title: Before controlled components
intro: A component is a reusable piece of a React screen. An input field is an element where a user enters information. State is information a component remembers between renders.

blocks.title: Component
blocks.text: A StudentName component can display a label, an input and a preview of the name.

blocks.title: Input field
blocks.text: A text input lets a student type. It has a value: the text currently displayed inside it.

blocks.title: State
blocks.text: useState gives us a stored value and a setter. Calling the setter requests a render using the new value.

key: State is remembered data that React can use to update the screen.
notes: Use three everyday pictures: a component is a small section of the page, an input is a writing space, and state is the component’s memory. Distinguish state from an ordinary local variable: React remembers state across renders and the setter requests another render. A component function can run again, but its state remains until React removes or resets that component. Transition to connecting state and input.

title: What makes an input controlled?
intro: A controlled input gets its displayed value from React state. When the student types, onChange updates that state, and React displays the new value.

blocks.title: value
blocks.text: Tells the input what text to display. It reads the name stored in state.

blocks.title: onChange
blocks.text: Reads the changed text and calls the setter. Without updating state, the displayed value stays the same.

blocks.title: Why use it?
blocks.text: The application always has the current value, so it can show a preview, validate it or enable a button.

key: value displays state; onChange updates state.
notes: Say: React is responsible for the input’s displayed text. The browser reports a change, but our handler must update the stored value. After the setter runs, React renders with the new value. A controlled text input should start with an empty string, not undefined, so it stays controlled. Explain that this is a loop, not two unrelated props. Transition to the complete StudentName component.

title: A complete student name input
intro: The input and the preview use the same state. This keeps the text the student sees consistent with the data React remembers.

blocks.title: Create state
blocks.text: name starts as an empty string. setName is the function used to change it.

blocks.title: Update on change
blocks.text: event.target.value contains the changed text. setName stores it for the next render.

blocks.title: Display the same value
blocks.text: value={name} displays the stored name; the paragraph shows the same name below the input.

key: One stored value can keep several parts of the screen in sync.
notes: Walk through the complete example from the import. The component begins with no name. The label is associated with the input through htmlFor and id. When a student types Sara, onChange receives an event and reads target.value. The setter schedules an update. React calls the component again with the new name, then both the input and preview use that value. Do not say the setter changes the old variable immediately; the updated value is available in the next render. Transition to following this loop one step at a time.

title: The controlled-input loop
intro: Imagine typing “S” into an empty name field. React uses the new state to keep the input and the name preview together.

blocks.title: Start
blocks.text: React creates the input with value="" from the initial state.

blocks.title: Change
blocks.text: Typing causes onChange. The handler reads "S" and calls setName("S").

blocks.title: Render again
blocks.text: React renders with name="S". The input’s value now displays "S". The same process repeats for the next letter.

key: Create input → type → detect change → update state → display state.
notes: Begin with the initial empty field. Split the first visual step into creating the input and the student typing, then follow the remaining stages. onChange detects the changed value, setName requests a state update, and the next render supplies the updated value. Ask students which prop reads state and which handler updates it. Mention that React can batch state updates and that the exact internal scheduling is not necessary for this lesson. Transition to validation.

title: Controlled inputs and validation
intro: Because React has the current value, it can check that value while the student edits. Validation means checking whether information follows the rules we need.

blocks.title: Check the current state
blocks.text: For example, name.trim().length > 0 checks that the name is not only empty spaces.

blocks.title: Use the result
blocks.text: Display a helpful message or disable Register while required information is missing.

blocks.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled
blocks.text: A controlled input uses state and value. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the browser and can be read when needed.

key: Controlled inputs make current values available; validation rules are still your job.
notes: Explain that trim removes spaces from the beginning and end before the length check. A state value does not validate itself; developers write the conditions. Controlled inputs are useful for live previews and immediate feedback, but not mandatory for every form. Uncontrolled inputs can also be validated and are useful for simpler forms. Avoid claiming uncontrolled inputs cannot validate until submission. Also explain that a client-side check is not enough for a real saved registration: the receiving service must check data too. Transition to the event object used in our handlers.

title: React gives us an event object
intro: A browser event is the browser’s record of an action. A SyntheticEvent is the event object React gives a handler, with a familiar interface for reading details and controlling the event.

blocks.title: What it means
blocks.text: React provides a convenient event object around the browser event. It is real event information, not a pretend action.

blocks.title: Why React provides it
blocks.text: Handlers can use a consistent set of properties and methods instead of dealing with many browser differences.

blocks.title: How to use it
blocks.text: Accept an event parameter in the handler, then read a property such as event.target.value.

key: SyntheticEvent is the event object React passes to your handler.
notes: Introduce the event object like a small information card about an action. It can say which element was involved, which kind of event occurred and, for a keyboard event, which key was used. The parameter name can be event or e; the object is the same idea. Different event types contain different useful details: key is useful for keyboard events, not a text-change event. Avoid unnecessary discussion of browser internals or old event pooling. Transition to the most useful properties.

title: Read useful event details
intro: Properties tell us what happened and where. The difference between target and currentTarget becomes especially useful when elements are nested.

blocks.title: event.target
blocks.text: The element where the event started. For a text input’s change handler, event.target.value is its changed text.

blocks.title: event.currentTarget
blocks.text: The element whose handler is running now. A card handler can run even if the event started on a button inside it.

blocks.title: event.type / event.key
blocks.text: type names the event, such as "click". key names the key for keyboard events, such as "Enter".

key: target = where it started. currentTarget = where this handler runs.
notes: Use a student search field: the change event begins in the input and its handler is on the input, so target and currentTarget are often the same there. Later, for a button inside a clickable card, target can be the button while currentTarget is the card. event.type identifies the event category; React’s text-input onChange can be backed by an input event, so do not promise its type is always change. Explain key only for keyboard events. Transition to the code that reads a changed search value.
code: // Place this inside a component’s returned JSX:

title: Elements, children and parents
intro: An HTML element is a part of a page, such as a button, a section or a form. A child is inside another element; that containing element is its parent.

blocks.title: Child button
blocks.text: An Add to Cart button is inside a product card.

blocks.title: Parent card
blocks.text: The card contains the button and may also respond to clicks, for example by opening product details.

blocks.title: Grandparent container
blocks.text: A container holds several cards. It is an ancestor of the button too.

key: Nested elements create the path an event can follow.
notes: Draw three nested boxes verbally or point to the process diagram. The button is a child of the card, and the card is a child of the container. Parent describes the directly containing element; ancestor includes parent, grandparent and higher containing elements. A handler can be attached to each of them. This product card is a familiar example to make nesting clear; the same pattern appears in student course cards. Transition to what happens when the inner button is clicked.

title: Why the card also gets a click
intro: For a bubbling event such as click, the event starts at the clicked element and then reaches its ancestors. Their click handlers can run too, unless propagation is stopped.

blocks.title: Button handler
blocks.text: The student clicks Add to Cart. The button handler adds the product.

blocks.title: Parent handler
blocks.text: The same click reaches the card. Its handler may open product details, which may not be what the student wanted.

blocks.title: Grandparent handler
blocks.text: The event can continue to the container. Bubbling lets a parent respond to actions from children without separate handlers everywhere.

key: Child button → parent card → grandparent container.
notes: Trace the upward path. This is one click being handled at several levels, not React creating new clicks for every box. Events follow the nested element structure. Bubbling can be helpful, for instance when one list handler responds to many items, but it can also trigger an unwanted parent action. Not every event behaves the same way; focus on click for this example. There is also a capture phase before the target, but we do not need its browser-internal details to understand bubbling. Transition to stopping the upward path.

title: Stop the parent click
intro: Call stopPropagation in the button handler when this click should not reach the card’s bubbling handler. The button’s own action still runs.

blocks.title: Stop the journey
blocks.text: event.stopPropagation() prevents this click from continuing to ancestor bubbling handlers.

blocks.title: Keep the button action
blocks.text: The next line still runs: the example shows an “Added to cart” alert.

blocks.title: What it does not do
blocks.text: It does not prevent normal browser actions. It also cannot undo a capture handler that already ran.

key: stopPropagation controls the event path, not the browser’s default action.
notes: Read the nesting in the code: an outer section has a click handler that opens details. The inner button has its own handler. First, the inner handler stops propagation; then it shows the added-to-cart response. The outer bubbling click handler does not run. These alerts demonstrate two distinct outcomes rather than implementing a real cart. type=button prevents accidental form submission if the card later sits in a form. Mention that capture handlers occur earlier and cannot be undone by this button handler. Transition to a different method: preventDefault.

title: preventDefault: stop browser action
intro: Some events have a normal browser action. A form submission may navigate or reload the page. preventDefault asks the browser not to perform that default action.

blocks.title: The normal action
blocks.text: Without handling it, the browser can send form data and navigate according to the form’s action and method.

blocks.title: The React response
blocks.text: Call preventDefault in onSubmit, then check the values and decide what the application should do.

blocks.title: What remains unchanged
blocks.text: The handler continues running. The event can still propagate unless you stop that separately.

key: preventDefault stops a default browser action; it does not stop bubbling.
notes: Return to the registration form. Explain that the browser has a built-in way to submit forms, often involving navigation. In a React application we may want to stay on the page and show validation or a result, so preventDefault blocks that normal action. It does not send the registration for us, nor does it stop the rest of our function. It works only when the event is cancelable. If a parent has a submit handler, propagation is a separate question. Transition to comparing both methods.

title: Two methods, two different jobs
intro: preventDefault changes what the browser normally does. stopPropagation changes which other elements receive the event. Sometimes a handler needs both, but they are not interchangeable.
key: Default action and event propagation are separate things.
notes: Give two questions. First: how do we keep a submitted registration form from navigating away? Answer: preventDefault. Second: how do we keep an Add to Cart click from triggering the card’s bubbling handler? Answer: stopPropagation. Ask whether preventDefault alone stops the card: no. Ask whether stopPropagation alone stops a form’s default submission: no. One handles browser behaviour, the other the event path. Transition to repeated actions and search performance.
table: Not the method for canceling submit
Does not stop the card handler

title: Should we search after every letter?
intro: Imagine searching for a student by typing their name. Starting a search after every change may do unnecessary work for queries the student has not finished.

blocks.title: Without a delay
blocks.text: Typing “Sara” can request results for “S”, “Sa”, “Sar” and “Sara”. The earlier results may not be useful.

blocks.title: Debouncing
blocks.text: Wait until the student stops typing for a short time, then run the search. A new change restarts the wait.

blocks.title: Why use it?
blocks.text: It reduces repeated work and requests. The field can still display each typed letter immediately.

key: Debouncing waits for the user to pause.
notes: Ask the question in the title before explaining the term. Use Sara as an illustrative typing sequence, not a measured performance statistic. The search can be delayed while the input value updates immediately, so typing still feels responsive. Waiting forever would be unhelpful: choose a short delay suited to the application. A debounce can fire after several separate pauses, not necessarily only once in an entire session. Transition to how a timer implements the wait.

title: Debounce: restart the timer
intro: A timer schedules a function to run later. setTimeout starts the wait; clearTimeout cancels a timer that has not fired yet.

blocks.title: A change starts a wait
blocks.text: The first letter starts a timer. If another letter arrives, cancel the old timer and start a new one.

blocks.title: A pause allows it to finish
blocks.text: After the last change, no replacement cancels the timer. The search runs after the waiting period.

blocks.title: Important limit
blocks.text: Canceling a timer does not cancel a request that has already started. Request cancellation is a separate task.

key: New change → cancel old timer → start a new wait.
notes: Explain all seven stages aloud: type a letter, start a timer, type another letter, cancel the previous timer, start a new timer, stop typing, then run the search after the delay. setTimeout schedules work; it does not freeze typing. clearTimeout needs the timer identifier returned by setTimeout. If a search has already started, clearing its old timer cannot stop the request. The actual timer may run slightly later if the browser is busy. Transition to a React effect that handles the timer cleanup.

title: Debounced student search
intro: This complete example filters a local list after a short pause. useEffect creates a timer when query changes and cleans up the previous timer.

blocks.title: Wait for the pause
blocks.text: setTimeout delays the result update by 300 milliseconds in this example.

blocks.title: Cancel the earlier wait
blocks.text: The returned cleanup calls clearTimeout before the next effect and when the component is removed.

blocks.title: Keep typing immediate
blocks.text: onChange updates query right away. Only updating the displayed results is delayed.

key: Update the field immediately; debounce the work that follows.
notes: Introduce the local names as demo data, not actual student records. useState stores the query and displayed matches. The effect depends on query, so every changed query schedules a new timer. Its cleanup cancels the previous timer before a new effect runs; React also cleans it up on unmount. After the pause, filter compares lower-case text and finds matching names. An empty query matches all names. No network request is made here. A real search might call a service and also protect against stale responses. The example uses 300 milliseconds as a teaching choice, not a required rule. Transition to scrolling, where waiting for a complete pause is often not what we want.

title: Throttling: limit repeated work
intro: Throttling limits how often a function runs while events keep happening. It is useful when we still want updates during an action, but not for every event.

blocks.title: Student-list example
blocks.text: Scrolling through a long student list can produce many scroll events close together.

blocks.title: Limit the handler
blocks.text: Allow a position update, then skip events until the chosen interval has passed.

blocks.title: Why use it?
blocks.text: It reduces repeated work while still showing progress during scrolling, rather than waiting for scrolling to stop.

key: Throttling controls how often the function runs.
notes: Contrast with the search example. During a long scroll, we may need to show how far down the list the student is. A debounce would wait for a pause; a throttle can keep giving limited updates during continuous activity. We limit the work inside the handler, not the browser’s normal scrolling. A throttled function runs only when eligible events happen; it is not necessarily a clock that fires on its own. Different throttle designs may include a final trailing call. Transition to a simple leading-only example.

title: Throttle a student-list scroll
intro: This leading-only example updates the displayed scroll position at most once per interval. It uses a ref to remember the last accepted event time.

blocks.title: Remember the time
blocks.text: useRef keeps last.current across renders without asking React to render when it changes.

blocks.title: Check the interval
blocks.text: If less than 200 milliseconds passed, return exits the handler. Otherwise, store the current time and update position.

blocks.title: Attach the handler
blocks.text: onScroll runs on the scrollable list. currentTarget.scrollTop gives that list’s scroll position.

key: This version skips extra events; it does not schedule a final update.
notes: Explain the import and the ref first. Initialising the ref to negative infinity lets the first event run. performance.now measures elapsed time; compare it with the last accepted time. return exits early for events inside the interval. When accepted, we store now and update state from the list’s scrollTop, so a paragraph can display it. The list style makes it scrollable. This is a leading-only throttle: if scrolling stops inside the interval, the last exact position may not be displayed. A library throttle with trailing behaviour can provide that final update. The 200 millisecond interval is only an example. Transition to deciding between debounce and throttle.

title: Debounce or throttle?
intro: Debouncing waits for a pause before running the work. Throttling allows work during ongoing activity, but limits how often it can run.

blocks.title: Choose debounce for search
blocks.text: The latest completed text matters most. Wait briefly after the student stops typing.

blocks.title: Choose throttle for scroll
blocks.text: Updates matter while the student is scrolling. Allow them at a limited rate.

blocks.title: Think before choosing
blocks.text: Ask: do I need the result after a pause, or do I need regular opportunities to update during the action?

key: Pause → debounce. Limited rate during activity → throttle.
notes: Restate both definitions before showing the next slide’s comparison table. Ask classmates to choose a method for searching names and then for updating a scroll-position indicator. Explain that the best choice depends on the experience, not just the event name: a scroll-end task could be debounced, while live scroll feedback could be throttled. These examples illustrate common uses, not universal rules. Transition to a direct comparison of the important differences.

title: Debouncing vs throttling
intro: Both reduce repeated work. Their main difference is when they allow the function to run.
key: Debouncing waits for the user to pause. Throttling controls how often the function runs.
notes: Explain each row, not just read it. Debounce restarts a waiting timer when a new event arrives. Throttle accepts an event only when the rate limit allows it. For debounce, pauses can produce multiple executions over time. For throttle, the exact first and last calls depend on the chosen leading and trailing options; our example used leading-only. Ask the class: if a student keeps typing without a long pause, what happens to the debounce timer? It keeps being replaced. Transition to a final recall exercise.

blocks.text: Which prop displays the stored value? Which handler updates it?

blocks.title: Form, card and search
blocks.text: Which method stops form navigation? Which stops the card click? Should name search debounce or throttle?

key: Explain the reason for your choice, not only the technical word.
notes: Let students answer before giving the solutions. Register uses onClick and passes the function; calling it during render runs it too early and can cause repeated updates. A controlled input displays state through value and updates it with onChange. preventDefault stops the form’s normal navigation; stopPropagation stops the card’s bubbling handler. Student name search is usually debounced because unfinished queries are less useful. Limited updates while scrolling are usually throttled. Transition to inviting questions.

blocks.text: The event starts the response; a handler can change state; React displays the updated information.

blocks.title: Event control
blocks.text: Use the event object to read details, prevent a default action or stop propagation when needed.

blocks.title: Repeated actions
blocks.text: Debounce waits for a pause. Throttle limits the rate while activity continues.

key: GROUP 8 · React Event Handling
notes: Thank your classmates and invite questions. Encourage them to describe an action from a website they use. Help them identify the event, the handler, whether state changes and whether there is a default browser action or bubbling to consider. If asked about performance, return to the difference between waiting for a pause and limiting a rate. The examples demonstrate React behaviour; real registration, cart and search services need separate saving or network logic. Close by repeating the memory tip for debounce and throttle.
